source.title: Disentangle Sample Size and Initialization Effect on Perfect Generalization for Single-Neuron Target
source.authors: Jiajie Zhao; Zhiwei Bai; Yaoyu Zhang

record.file_problem: Full paper text supplied, including appendices; no apparent cutoff or garbling that prevents extraction.
record.tranche_reason: Empirically tests generalization in a different, highly simplified setting: two-layer networks recovering a single-neuron target, with initialization scale and sample size varied. Its measures and setup differ from the catalog versions' natural-label classification and other specified interventions.
record.gate_note: The study reports recovery/generalization error across initialization scales, sample sizes, and widths. Its main target is a single-neuron function generated by the same target function, rather than natural labels, random-label memorization, or test error on classification benchmarks. The reported one-neuron activity observations are not measurements of any listed version's claim about generalization measures.
record.test_reason: The study measures synthetic single-neuron recovery under changes in initialization, sample size and width. None of its results tests V1–V8. In particular, its width experiment reports low error across widths, without establishing that widening beyond interpolation keeps lowering test error.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is accurate: in this simplified target-recovery setting, smaller initialization and larger sample sizes tend to improve generalization, while initialization imbalance and sample-size thresholds govern recovery. These are empirical findings in a restricted setting; the authors acknowledge simplicity and assumed convergence to a local minimum.
record.recipe_differences: Synthetic single-neuron function recovery with two-layer fully connected networks and gradient descent; varies initialization and sample size, rather than natural-label classification or the interventions in the listed versions.
record.method_sensitivity: Generalization/recovery varies with initialization scale, initialization imbalance ratio, sample size, and sampled dataset; the fixed evenly spaced and random-sampling experiments show different sample-size trends.

fits_no_version.finding: Recovery depends on initialization imbalance and sample size; in the one-dimensional experiment, two samples fail, three allow recovery only at special ratios, and six permit recovery across tested small initializations.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: For synthetic single-neuron recovery, sample size and initialization imbalance jointly determine whether training recovers the target.

fits_no_version.finding: With Gaussian sampling, mean generalization error decreases with sample size, with greater improvement at smaller initialization scales.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Smaller initialization and more samples can improve generalization in synthetic single-neuron recovery.

fits_no_version.finding: Under small initialization, matched imbalance ratios produce aligned parameter trajectories across initialization scales.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Initial relative neuron magnitudes govern limiting training trajectories under small initialization.

fits_no_version.finding: The varying-width tanh experiment reports low error and concentration of substantial weights in a subset of neurons.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Wide networks can attain low synthetic target-recovery error while relatively few neurons contribute substantially.

record.problems: The study is confined to recovering a single-neuron target with synthetic data and does not test natural-label classification or random-label memorization. Many plotted outcomes lack numerical values in the text. It reports limited seed counts in several experiments, and the authors state that the experimental framework is simple and that convergence to a local minimum is assumed rather than proved in Theorem 2.

untested.parts: No comparison of random-label fitting with natural-label generalization or chance-level held-out performance.
No demonstration that widening beyond the width needed to interpolate continually lowers test error.
No convolutional versus fully connected architecture comparison.
No adaptive optimizer versus SGD comparison.
No batch-size intervention or fixed-epoch comparison.
No magnitude-aware sharpness measurement or ranking of generalization-gap predictors.
No removal of memorized examples and retraining comparison.

record.verdict_notes: States are cannot_determine relative to V1–V8 because all rows link to none; this does not negate the reported recovery outcomes. No verdict-bearing results are missing. The introduction cites original generalization studies but does not test their listed claims.

versions.untested_parts: Does not compare fitting random labels with generalizing on natural labels.
Varies width in one experiment, but does not test widening one-hidden-layer ReLU networks beyond the interpolation threshold or report the version's MNIST/CIFAR setting.
Does not compare convolutional and fully connected architectures on image classification.
Uses gradient descent, but does not compare adaptive optimizers with SGD.
Does not vary batch size or test large-batch training.
Does not measure magnitude-aware sharpness or compare generalization-gap measures.
Does not remove or retrain on memorized examples.

rows.note: Tracks initialization dynamics, not a listed version's generalization-gap measure.
rows.check: Trajectory agreement does not measure a listed version. Curves were translated in time to align them; agreement should be described with that condition.

rows.subject: two-layer neural network with activation σ(x) = x/(1 + x²), target y = tanh(x + 1)
rows.operation_detail: Measured parameter trajectories and generalization error after training on six evenly spaced points.
rows.measure: parameter trajectories and final generalization error
rows.value: The generalization error is significantly low in an overparameterized network.
rows.locator: Section 7, Figures 5 and 6 and accompanying text
rows.note: The accompanying explanation attributes low error partly to most neurons having minimal weights relative to the largest-weight neuron; exact error values are only plotted.
rows.check: Conflates two experiments. Figure 5 uses width 1000, rational activation and six samples to examine trajectories. Figure 6 uses tanh, varying widths and three samples; the low-generalization-error statement refers to Figure 6(b). Separate these results.

rows.check: Section 7 explicitly describes low generalization error for Figure 6(b), so the result is not entirely figure-only. It gives no monotonic decrease with width or interpolation-threshold comparison needed for V2.

conditions.value: inputs drawn independently from uniform distribution on [-2, 2]^d
generalization error on 1000 independently drawn uniform points

rows.value: When sample size is larger than optimistic sample size, the network can recover at c̃ = 1 or c̃ = 0; when sample size is above separation sample size of Q1, all initialization can recover target function.
rows.locator: Appendix B, Figures 9 and 10 and accompanying text
rows.note: The authors state that recovery is not guaranteed merely by reaching the optimistic or separation sample size; at n = 6 there is a small probability of failure near c̃ = 0.
rows.check: Does not measure a listed version. Split sample-size conditions if retaining recovery states; failures near zero imbalance occur at n = 6–8. Training budgets also differ: 1e6 iterations for n = 5–8 and 2e7 for n = 9–10.
